credits.creator: Samira Mian
credits.note: The rosette at the centre (inner circle from one chord, star lines joining its points 150° apart) follows her construction.

credits.source: Drawing of the Bou Inania pattern
credits.creator: @aslam.geometricpatterns
credits.note: Every line beyond the rosette was read from this drawing; the construction through crossings is our own reconstruction.

credits.source: Zellige of the Bou Inania madrasa, Fès (photograph, Wikimedia Commons)

given.A: Any point to the right of O. OA is the radius of the first circle.

steps.text: Rule a horizontal line through O and A and draw the first circle about O through A. Keep this opening.

Put the compass point where the circle meets the line on the right, and draw a circle through O; do the same on the left. Rule the vertical through O, and draw the same circle about its top and bottom points.

The four circles cut the first one at eight more points: it is divided into twelve. Rule the lines through O and opposite points, then halve every angle between them, so there is a line through O every 15°.
steps.textWithoutHelpers: The four circles cut the first one at eight more points: it is divided into twelve. Rule the lines through O and opposite points, then halve the angles between them where the pattern needs a line: at 45°, 75° and 135°.

steps.text: Halve the angles between the lines at 0° and 15°, and at 15° and 30°: two more lines through O, at 7.5° and 22.5°.
Mark where the 75° line cuts the circle and join that point to the point on the left of the horizontal. Where this chord crosses the vertical, draw a circle about O: Samira Mian’s inner circle.
steps.textWithoutHelpers: Mark where the 75° line cuts the circle and join that point to the point on the left of the horizontal. Where this chord crosses the vertical, draw a circle about O: Samira Mian’s inner circle.

steps.text: Mark where the inner circle meets the lines at 0°, 30°, 60° and so on, and join each of these points to the one 150° round. The twelve lines make the twelve-pointed star (set A).

Draw circles of the first size about the points at 0° and 30°. They cross outside the first circle on the 15° line: the bigger circle about O passes through that crossing. Through it, rule the line at right angles to the horizontal, and turn it round: the big twelve-sided figure (set E).
The ring of small stars and pentagons.
steps.textWithoutHelpers: The ring of small stars and pentagons.

parts.text: Where a star line crosses a side of the big figure, rule a line at right angles to the 7.5° line, and its mirror image in the horizontal. Turn both round: 24 lines that make the small five-pointed stars.
Through the point of the first circle at 30°, rule the line at right angles to the 30° line: it just touches the circle. Turn it round. These are helper lines.
Where the helper lines touching the circle at 30° and −30° cross the horizontal, rule a line at right angles to it, and turn it round: these lines close the pentagons.

steps.text: The octagon of the corner stars, and the frame.

parts.text: Where a side of the big figure crosses one of the 24 lines, rule a line at right angles to the 22.5° line. Turn it round in eighths: the octagon of the corner stars.
Where an octagon side crosses one of the 24 lines, rule a line at right angles to the horizontal. Turn it round in quarters: the frame, and the edge of the tile.
Where a star line crosses a pentagon line, rule a line at right angles to the horizontal, and turn it round: the inner side of the ring.
Where two of the 24 lines cross on the horizontal, rule a line at right angles to the 15° line, and turn it round: the points of the ring.
Where a side of the big figure crosses the inner side of the ring, rule a line at right angles to the horizontal, and turn it round. These carry the star lines on into the corners.
Where the frame crosses a pentagon line, rule a line at right angles to the 45° line, and turn it round in quarters: the lines across the corners.
Where a side of the big figure crosses a pentagon line, rule a line at right angles to the 15° line, and turn it round.
Where two of the 24 lines cross on the 45° line, rule a line at right angles to the 15° line, and turn it round.

steps.text: An eight-pointed star at each corner of the frame. Its square is the little square between the big figure’s sides and the frame.
steps.textWithoutHelpers: An eight-pointed star at each corner of the frame. Its square is the little square between the big figure’s sides and the frame.

parts.text: Join the little square’s other two corners, and mark where that line crosses the diagonal: the star’s centre.
Through the centre, rule a level line and an upright one. Where they meet the line across the corner are two points of the diamond.
Draw the circle about the centre through one of these points: it meets the level and upright lines again at the other two.
Join the four points: the diamond, which with the little square makes the eight-pointed star.

steps.text: Mark the corners of the pattern: every point where the pattern turns or ends. Where the inner band on the right (or top) side breaks, rule a line across to the left (or bottom) side: the band breaks there too, because the next tile lies over it.

The panel: the frame’s square, with its band on all four sides. It repeats by sliding one band less than its width, so each copy’s band lies on its neighbour’s band. The repeating tile is the square between the frame’s left and bottom sides and the big figure’s right and top sides: it holds the band on two sides only.

ink.text: Ink the twelve-pointed star and its petals, the ring of small stars and pentagons, the ring round the shields, and the bands and corner stars out to the frame. At the end, the panels around it slide out in blue, each overlapping this one by a band: each of their lines meets this tile’s edge just where one of its own lines carries on, and the band breaks there to let it through.

pattern.text: Repeat the square edge to edge: neighbouring tiles share the frame band, and the corner pieces of four tiles meet in an eight-pointed star.
